<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par143 />{{GHGmargin-letter|143|b}}
(''b'') An independent verbal-clause: (α) with a retrospective suffix,<ref>Cf. the Mêšaʿ inscription, l. 31, ''and Ḥoronain'', ''therein dwelt'', &c.</ref> e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=6}} (cf. {{GHGpar|116|w}}); 17:15 ''as for Sarai thy wife, thou shalt not call her name Sarai''; 26:15, 28:13, 34:8, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=30|verse=37}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=10|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=9|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=11|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=33|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=9|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=11|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=46|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=65|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=74|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=1|verse=17}}; with a pronoun as the principal subject, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=27}}; (β) without a retrospective suffix, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=19|verse=17}} ''every one'' that ''mentions it'' (Judah) ''to it'' (Egypt), ''it'' (Egypt) ''is afraid''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|143|c}}
Rem. 1. In all the above examples prominence is given to the principal subject (by its mere separation from the context by means of a greater disjunctive, as a ''casus pendens''<ref>But this term must not (any more than that formerly used ‘the subject preceding ''absolutely''’) be misunderstood to mean that the principal subject is, as it were, floating in the air, and that the whole sentence results in an anacoluthon. On the contrary, to the Semitic mind, such sentences appear quite as correctly formed as ordinary noun- and verbal-clauses.</ref>) in a manner which would be quite impossible in a simple noun or verbal-clause (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=1|verse=3}} if it were {{GHGheb|text=דֶּ֫רֶךְ יְהֹוָה בְּסוּפָה}}); cf. the French ''c’est moi qu’on a accusé''. But the statement or question contained in the clause which forms the predicate also receives greater weight. For the same purpose other members of the sentence also are sometimes placed at the beginning and resumed again by a following suffix; thus the object, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=35|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=47|verse=21|hidebook=1}} (with the Samaritan and LXX read perhaps {{GHGheb|text=הֶֽעֱבִיד}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=29}}; a specification of place, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=22|verse=18}}, &c.; a substantive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=6|verse=23}}; cf. the examples in {{GHGpar|135|a}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=15|verse=29}} a dative is co-ordinated with the ''casus pendens'', i.e. there is a transition to a different construction.

{{GHGmargin-letter|143|d}}
2. To compound sentences belong also the numerous examples already treated in the account of the tenses, where the predicate of a ''casus pendens'' is introduced by the {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}}. The isolation and prominence of the principal subject is in this case still more marked than in the instances treated above; on the ''casus pendens'' with a following imperfect consecutive (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=6|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=33|verse=24|hidebook=1}}), cf. {{GHGpar|111|h}}; with a following perfect consecutive (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=4|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=44|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=9|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=56|verse=6|hidebook=1}} f.), {{GHGpar|112|t}} and ''mm''; on the participle as ''casus pendens'', {{GHGpar|112|oo}} and {{GHGpar|116|w}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=17}} {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}} follows with the cohortative; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=115|verse=7}}, the imperfect is separated by {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} from the {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=4|verse=6}} as for ''thy hope'', it is ''the integrity of thy ways'', 36:26, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=5|verse=6}}, an incomplete noun-clause is appended by {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}}. On {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}} after disconnected specifications of time, cf. {{GHGpar|112|oo}} at the end, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=34}} {{GHGheb|text=וְעַתָּה וַֽאֲנִי עַבְדֶּ֫ךָ|translate=and now}} (so far as the present is concerned) ''I will be thy servant'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=12|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=4|verse=1}} (''me thou needest not fear'').

{{GHGmargin-letter|143|e}}
3. Sometimes a substantive introduced by {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} (''in respect to''; cf. {{GHGpar|119|u}}) serves the same purpose as the ''casus pendens'' beginning the sentence, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=18|verse=8}} (unless the {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} here serves to introduce the object, according to {{GHGpar|117|n}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=32|verse=1}} (where, however, {{GHGheb|text=וְשָׂרִים}} should most probably be read); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=9|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=7|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=24|verse=20|hidebook=1}} ff., {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=7|verse=21}}. On the other hand, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=16|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=17|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=32|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=89|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=119|verse=91|hidebook=1}}, are very doubtful. The suggestion of P. Haupt ({{GHGcite|title=Johns Hopkins University Circulars}}, xiii. no. 114; Baltimore, 1894) also deserves attention, that in passages like {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=9|verse=4}}, and in {{GHGheb|text=לְכֹל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=27|verse=3}}, 19, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=44|verse=9}}, &c., {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} is not the preposition, but an emphasizing particle, answering to the Arab. ''lă, surely''; Assyrian ''lû''; with {{GHGheb|text=כֹּל}} it is equivalent to ''in short.'' Cf. also {{GHGheb|text=לְ־לְ}} ''sive—sive, et—et'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=17|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=1|verse=11}}, Assyrian ''lû''—''lû''.<section end=par143 /><noinclude>
